h1: Pairing whisky with Indian food, from kebabs to mithai
title: Pairing Whisky with Indian Food | Craft Beer School
desc: How to pair whisky with Indian food, from smoky tandoori kebabs and rich curries to mithai, with simple rules and suggestions to try.
teaser: Peated whisky with tandoori chicken. Sherried malt with rogan josh. Bourbon with gulab jamun. Start there.
standfirst: Whisky and Indian food can work beautifully together if you match weight, smoke and sweetness and treat chilli heat with respect. Here is how to start, with dishes most of us already love.
sections: Why pair whisky with food at all

Whisky is usually drunk before or after a meal in India, often with soda and snacks. Drunk with food, a well-chosen whisky can bring out flavours in a dish and the dish can soften the whisky. The trick is to think about weight, flavour and heat rather than strict rules.

Pairings here are suggestions, not laws. Your own palate wins every time. Our guide to whisky tasting for beginners is a good place to start if you are new to whisky itself.

• Match weight. Light, fruity whiskies suit lighter dishes. Rich, sherried or peated whiskies suit heavier food.
  • Echo or contrast flavours. Smoke with tandoor char works by echo. A crisp, fruity whisky against creamy butter chicken works by contrast.
  • Respect chilli heat. Alcohol makes chilli burn more intensely. With fiery dishes, add water or soda to the whisky, or choose a lower strength.

A highball made with soda and ice is often the easiest whisky to drink with spicy food.

Smoke and char from the tandoor pair naturally with peated whisky. Try tandoori chicken, seekh kebabs or tandoori pomfret with a lightly peated malt. The smoke in the glass echoes the char on the plate.

Lucknowi galouti kebabs, soft and gently spiced, suit a smooth ex-bourbon matured malt with honey and vanilla notes. For paneer tikka, a light, fruity whisky or a highball keeps things fresh. Our guide to beer and tandoori pairing uses the same thinking for beer.

Rich, slow-cooked dishes such as Kashmiri rogan josh or Hyderabadi mutton dishes stand up to sherry matured whisky. Dried fruit and spice in the whisky sit well with cardamom, cinnamon and clove in the gravy. Add a splash of water to soften the alcohol.

Creamy dishes like butter chicken or korma suit a lighter whisky that cuts through richness, or a whisky highball. Coastal dishes with coconut and tamarind, such as a Goan xacuti or a Kerala fish curry, can be hard to pair. A fruity, unpeated malt with water is a safe start.

Pakoras, samosas and chakli are classic whisky companions for a reason. Fried, salty food pairs well with a highball, as the soda and ice refresh the palate. Chaat and pani puri, with their sweet, sour and spicy layers, can overwhelm most whiskies, so keep those for a simple highball or a soft drink.

Roasted cashews, masala peanuts and cheese are easy partners for almost any whisky.

Sweet dishes are where whisky can really shine. Gulab jamun with its syrup and cardamom works well with bourbon or a sherried malt. Kaju katli and other nut sweets suit a nutty, oloroso style whisky. Dark chocolate with a peated whisky is a classic combination worth trying.

Match sweetness with care. A very sweet dessert can make a dry whisky taste thin and harsh. Choose a richer, sweeter style whisky with desserts.

India's regional cuisines give plenty of room to experiment. Try a smoky malt with Naga pork with bamboo shoot, where smoke meets smoke. Try a fruity Indian single malt with Chettinad pepper chicken, adding water to tame the pepper. A soft blend with soda suits Bengali fish fry or Mangalorean prawn ghee roast, where the soda cuts the richness.

Rajasthani laal maas, fiery with red chilli, is a tough match. Treat it like any very hot dish: a long highball, plenty of water and a cooling raita on the side. For Punjabi dishes like amritsari fish or dal makhani, a smooth, honeyed whisky with a little water is an easy start. Write down which combinations work for you. Your notes will soon be more useful than any list.

Pour small measures, around 15 to 30 ml, when pairing with food. Keep water on the table for diluting the whisky and for drinking. Taste the whisky alone first, then with a bite. Notice how each changes.

Whisky with food is about enjoyment, not volume. Make sure guests who do not drink have something good to drink too, such as a fresh lime soda or a spiced buttermilk. Nobody should drive after drinking, however good the meal was.
faqs: What whisky goes with tandoori chicken?
A lightly peated malt is a good start, as the smoke echoes the tandoor char. A whisky highball also works well.
Can whisky be paired with spicy Indian food?
Yes, with care. Alcohol makes chilli heat feel stronger, so add water or soda to the whisky or choose a lower strength.
What whisky goes with Indian sweets?
Richer, sweeter styles such as bourbon or sherry matured malts suit mithai like gulab jamun and kaju katli.
